title: Modularization strategy
scopeHtml: Why and when to modularize, module types and layouts, api/impl splits, dependency direction, composition root, navigation and shared modules, granularity, visibility, convention plugins, dynamic features, enforcement and migration. (Build-time metrics live in chunk 08; Hilt specifics in chunk 10; navigation internals in chunk 12.)

questions.promptHtml: Why would you split an Android app into multiple Gradle modules, and when would you decide not to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you see modularization as a cost-bearing tool with specific payoffs, or as a fashion ("NiA does it").

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A Gradle module is a compilation and visibility boundary. I split to get enforced boundaries, parallel and incremental builds, clear ownership per team, reuse across apps (phone, Wear, TV) and optional delivery through Play Feature Delivery. I don't split when the codebase is small and one team owns it: every module adds configuration, boilerplate and sync time, and the benefits don't show up below a certain size."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First principles: in a single-module app, every class sees every other public or internal class, so boundaries exist only as convention. A module changes that: a class in :feature:cart literally cannot reference :feature:profile unless the Gradle dependency is declared, and internal hides symbols from the rest of the build.

The Android guide lists the payoffs: reusability, strict visibility control, customizable delivery (strong reasons: a necessity if you need them), then scalability, ownership, encapsulation, testability and build time (achievable by other means, modularization enforces them).

Monolith                       Modularized
:app (everything)              :app -> :feature:a -> :core:data -> :core:model
change 1 file -> recompile     change 1 file -> recompile only that module
 whole :app (sequential)       + dependents; independent modules build in parallel

When NOT to: under roughly one team and a codebase that builds incrementally in under a minute, the gain is mostly theoretical. The guide itself warns about "too complex": if the project will not grow past a threshold, scalability and build gains won't apply. Costs: more build.gradle.kts files to keep consistent, slower Gradle configuration (per-project cost), more boilerplate for exposing APIs, harder refactors across boundaries, and slower IDE sync.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// settings.gradle.kts: the boundary is declared, not implied
include(":app", ":feature:cart", ":feature:profile", ":core:data", ":core:model")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Modularizing "for build speed" without measuring: a clean build gets no faster, and incremental builds only improve if dependencies are narrow.
  • Treating module count as a quality metric.
  • Splitting by technical layer only (all UI in :ui) which preserves the monolith's coupling.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you get boundaries without modules? → Partly: packages plus lint/Konsist rules enforce convention, but internal and compile-time dependency denial only come from modules.
  2. What is the cheapest first step? → Extract a leaf :core:model or design-system module, no behavior risk, and measure.
  3. At what size does it pay off? → No universal number; I look at incremental build time, number of teams touching the same files and merge-conflict rate rather than lines of code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "faster builds and cleaner code." Senior: names which benefit they are buying (boundaries vs parallelism vs delivery), the break-even signals, and the ongoing cost of keeping many modules consistent.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that modularized at 150k LOC with 3 devs spent a quarter on plumbing; teams at 1M LOC with 8 squads saw merge conflicts in :app drop sharply after feature extraction.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the typical module types in a modern multi-module Android app and what goes in each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the standard vocabulary (app, feature, data, core) and the dependency shape between them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The app module is the entry point and wires everything. Feature modules hold a screen or flow: UI, ViewModel, navigation entry. Data modules own a domain's repository, data sources and models, and hide the sources. Core or common modules hold shared things: design system, network client, analytics, utilities. Features depend on data and core, never on each other; the app depends on features."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
This mirrors the official guidance (Now in Android style).

                 :app
          /       |        \
 :feature:home  :feature:cart  :feature:profile
        \          |          /
         :core:data (repositories)  :core:ui / :core:designsystem
                 |
        :core:network  :core:database  :core:model
  • App module: Application, MainActivity, root NavHost, DI graph assembly, build variants/flavors. If you target Wear/TV/Auto, one app module per target.
  • Feature module: associated with screens, so it has UI plus ViewModel. A feature can be several screens (checkout flow). Feature modules depend on data modules.
  • Data module: repository as the public API, data sources hidden with internal/private.
  • Common/core modules: UI kit, analytics, network client, utilities. They represent no layer, which is why they need curation (see the god-module question).
  • Test modules: shared fakes and test data.

Prefer pure Kotlin/Java library modules over Android library modules where no Android resources or manifest are needed: the Android guide notes Android modules carry extra overhead (AAR packaging, resource processing).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :feature:cart/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":core:data"))
    implementation(project(":core:designsystem"))
    // never: implementation(project(":feature:profile"))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting the Retrofit/Room implementation types in the module's public surface, so features compile against them.
  • A :core:common that accumulates everything.
  • Domain modules in a layer-per-module design that force every feature change to touch three modules.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does a domain/use-case layer go? → Optional; either inside data/feature or a :core:domain pure-Kotlin module when multiple features share business rules.
  2. Why one app module per device type? → Isolates platform-specific dependencies and manifests.
  3. Where do models live? → :core:model as a pure Kotlin leaf is common, but only for models truly shared; feature-private UI models stay inside the feature.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists the boxes. Senior explains arrows (who may depend on whom), what each module hides, and which boxes are optional for a given team size.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team with :data, :domain, :ui as three giant modules still had every PR touching all three; moving to per-feature vertical slices cut cross-team review noise.

questions.promptHtml: In Gradle, what is the difference between api and implementation for a module dependency, and which should you default to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core mechanism behind encapsulation and incremental builds; weak candidates only know "implementation is faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "implementation keeps a dependency off my consumers' compile classpath; api exports it. I default to implementation and use api only when a type from that dependency appears in my module's public signatures, like a supertype or a public parameter. Both are on the runtime classpath either way."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the Gradle Java Library docs: api dependencies are part of the library's public interface and show up on consumers' compile classpath; implementation dependencies stay internal, available to consumers only at runtime. Benefits: fewer accidental dependencies, smaller compile classpath, and less recompilation (changing an implementation dependency doesn't force consumers to recompile as they never saw it at compile time).

Example: :core:data exposes UserRepository returning User (from :core:model). Consumers need User at compile time, so :core:data must declare api(project(":core:model")). But Retrofit is used only inside, so implementation(libs.retrofit).

:feature -> :core:data --api--> :core:model     (feature compiles against model)
                      --impl--> retrofit         (feature cannot see retrofit types)

If you wrongly use implementation for something exposed in a public signature, consumers fail to compile with "Cannot access class X. Check your module classpath", which is the system working.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core:data/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    api(project(":core:model"))          // User appears in public API
    implementation(libs.retrofit)       // hidden detail
    implementation(libs.room.runtime)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using api everywhere "to avoid compile errors": every change in a leaf now recompiles the whole tree and the module graph becomes implicit.
  • Assuming implementation hides code at runtime; it doesn't.
  • Forgetting that Kotlin inline functions or annotations can force a dependency to be visible (compiler may need class files for types in private members; Gradle docs suggest compileOnlyApi or api).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does this affect recompilation concretely? → With implementation, a ABI-affecting change in a transitive leaf recompiles only direct dependents of it, not the whole upstream chain.
  2. What is compileOnly? → Available at compile time only, not packaged; used for annotations or stubs.
  3. api on project() vs on a library? → Same rules; project api chains make module graphs effectively transitive, which is why teams audit with the dependency-analysis plugin.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "implementation is faster". Senior: public-signature test, compile vs runtime classpath, and the ABI consequence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An api(project(":core:network")) in :core:data made all 40 features import OkHttp types directly; swapping the HTTP stack later became a 40-module change.

questions.promptHtml: What rules govern which module may depend on which, and why can't Gradle modules have cycles?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Directionality is the whole point of modularization; cycles reveal design problems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Dependencies point one way: app to features, features to data/core, core to leaves, and features never depend on other features. Gradle refuses cycles because a module must be compiled before its dependents; with A needing B and B needing A there is no valid build order. A cycle is a design signal: extract the shared piece or invert the dependency."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Gradle builds a project dependency DAG. For compilation, A's output (classes/AAR) is an input for B. A cycle gives "Circular dependency between the following tasks" errors. Rules of thumb:

app -> feature -> data -> core(network, db, model)
          \________________/ never upward, never sideways
  • Higher-level policy (features) may depend on lower-level (data/core).
  • Siblings don't depend on each other; they communicate via a mediator (navigation in app) or through a shared lower module (see Q155).
  • Cycle breakers: (1) move the shared types to a lower module, (2) dependency inversion (interface in an api module, implementation elsewhere), (3) merge modules if they truly are one system (the guide's tip: if two modules rely heavily on each other's knowledge, they may be one).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: cycle
// :feature:cart  -> implementation(project(":feature:profile"))
// :feature:profile -> implementation(project(":feature:cart"))   // error

// Fixed: shared contract in a lower module
// :feature:cart  -> :feature:profile:api
// :feature:profile:impl -> :feature:profile:api

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixing" a cycle by moving classes into :core:common until it compiles (dumping ground).
  • Allowing :core modules to depend on :feature modules.
  • Thinking only direct cycles matter; transitive ones fail the same way.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you find who creates the cycle? → Gradle error names tasks; ./gradlew :app:dependencies or a module-graph plugin visualizes it.
  2. Cycle between a feature and the app? → Features must never reference :app; move shared bits down or pass via DI/navigation.
  3. Is it OK for :core:data to depend on :core:database and :core:network? → Yes, leaf-ward; keep core siblings from depending on each other unless clearly layered.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior treats cycle errors as architecture feedback and names the three breakers rather than shuffling classes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "temporary" dependency from :core:analytics to a feature module for a screen-name enum blocked extraction of that feature for a year.

questions.promptHtml: What is the "composition root" idea and why is the :app module usually that place in a multi-module app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of where concrete implementations are chosen and why features stay unaware of them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A composition root is the one place where concrete implementations are chosen and wired. In a multi-module app, :app depends on everything, so it can bind api interfaces to impl classes, assemble navigation and build variants, while feature modules only know contracts."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Android guide's dependency inversion section: the feature module depends on an abstraction module; the implementation module also depends on the abstraction; the app module supplies the implementation, even per variant (releaseImplementation vs debugImplementation vs androidTestImplementation).

:feature:cart --> :payments:api <-- :payments:impl
                       ^                  ^
                       +------ :app ------+  (selects impl, DI graph assembled here)

With Hilt, the DI graph is assembled by the Hilt plugin in :app which aggregates all @Module/@InstallIn in the classpath; features don't reference the generated component. Also in :app: root NavHost aggregating each feature's graph, Application, manifest merging, flavors, signing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :app/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":feature:cart"))
    implementation(project(":payments:impl"))   // only app sees impl
    debugImplementation(project(":payments:fake"))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting :feature modules depend on :impl modules "just this once".
  • Putting business logic in :app because it's convenient.
  • Forgetting that an impl module not on the app classpath means missing bindings only at Hilt/Dagger compile time or runtime (Koin).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does :app need api or implementation on features? → implementation; nobody consumes :app.
  2. How do you test a feature without :app? → Provide fakes in a test source set or fake impl module.
  3. What breaks if two impls are on the classpath? → Duplicate bindings at DI compile time (Dagger/Hilt) or last-wins in Koin; use variants or qualifiers deliberately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links composition root to dependency inversion and per-variant impl swapping, not just "app has MainActivity".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Debug builds swapped in a fake payments impl via debugImplementation; a missing releaseImplementation shipped a release without a binding and failed at Hilt compile time (caught in CI, not production).

questions.promptHtml: What is an api/impl module split for a feature, what problem does it solve, and when is it overkill?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes dependency inversion at module level and awareness of its cost (2x modules).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I split a feature into :feature:x:api with the public contract (interfaces, navigation keys, small models) and :feature:x:impl with UI, ViewModel, data. Other features depend only on api, so they never recompile when impl changes and can't reach into internals. It solves feature-to-feature coupling and build fan-out, but doubles module count, so I use it only where cross-feature dependencies exist, not by default."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Android modularization docs say separate API and implementation when: multiple implementations make sense, multiple apps share capabilities, independent teams, or a large codebase. The build benefit is real: changes in impl don't force dependents of api to recompile because the api ABI is unchanged.

Rules (from NiA docs on navigation modularization): api of feature A should not depend on another feature's api or impl; impl may depend on another feature's api only.

:feature:orders:impl ---> :feature:profile:api (open profile screen)
:feature:profile:impl --> :feature:profile:api
:app --> all impls

What goes into api: navigation keys/routes, a facade interface (ProfileLauncher), shared value objects. What doesn't: ViewModels, repositories, composables of screens.

Cost: twice the modules, twice the build files, and DI bindings spanning modules. Overkill when the feature is only used by :app: nobody else needs the contract.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :feature:profile:api
@Serializable data class ProfileKey(val userId: String)
interface ProfileEntryPoint { fun profileEntry(): NavEntryProvider }

// :feature:orders:impl build file
dependencies { implementation(project(":feature:profile:api")) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting everything into api, defeating the purpose.
  • Creating api modules for features no other module references.
  • api modules that pull heavy dependencies (Retrofit, Room) onto consumers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does impl get bound to api consumers? → DI in :app: impl provides the binding, consumers inject the interface.
  2. Naming: :feature:profile:api vs :feature:profile-api? → Gradle path nesting of a module that is also a parent project has pitfalls; convention is a team choice, verify folder/plugin implications.
  3. Alternative to api modules? → A single :navigation module of keys (tradeoff: central module change recompiles everyone).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states when not to do it and keeps api tiny and dependency-free.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Orders needed a "view profile" action; without profile:api the team added implementation(project(":feature:profile")), and every profile UI change rebuilt orders and its tests.

questions.contextHtml: You join a startup: single :app module, 180k LOC Kotlin, 6 Android engineers split across Checkout, Search and Account. Incremental debug build takes ~95 s (clean ~7 min). Three engineers touch OrderViewModel weekly, and merge conflicts in shared util files happen daily. Product wants to add a Wear OS app in 6 months. The CTO says "NiA is modular, let's go full multi-module with api/impl everywhere in one sprint."
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond and what do you actually do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, modularize everything, one module per class group." Or the opposite: "No, it adds overhead." Neither names the signal, order of extraction, or measurement.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the actual pain: build time, conflicts, or ownership? (decides where to cut). Is the Wear app confirmed? (reuse driver). How is incremental build time distributed: kapt/KSP or Compose? (a module split won't fix annotation processing in one hot module). Team growth plan? Release cadence constraints?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No incident, but I'd get a baseline: ./gradlew assembleDebug --scan for cached vs not tasks, --profile, number of merge conflicts per week.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) build time dominated by KAPT/Hilt in one big module, fixable partly by KSP; (b) conflicts concentrated in util and OrderViewModel; (c) Wear reuse needs :core:model and :core:data extracted.
  4. How I'd verify each: Build scan task timeline; git log for most-changed files; module-graph plan sketch.
  5. Root cause: Monolith with weak boundaries: any change recompiles all, ownership unclear.
  6. Fix: Short-term: no big bang. Step 1 extract :core:model, :core:designsystem, :core:data (needed for Wear anyway). Step 2 extract the most conflicted feature (Checkout) as a pilot with a convention plugin. Step 3 re-measure; continue only if incremental builds and conflicts improved. Long-term: ~8-12 modules, not 60. api/impl only where cross-feature links exist.
  7. Prevention: convention plugins from day one, a module-creation checklist, lint/Konsist checks for dependency direction.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not one sprint, not api/impl everywhere (doubles modules with 6 devs), not layer-based modules.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Wear dropped from roadmap? → I'd still extract data/core if conflicts persist; otherwise pause after the pilot.
  • Build time didn't improve after the pilot? → Check configuration time and kapt; modules don't help if everything depends on a giant :core.
  • A dev wants one module per screen? → Granularity pitfall: overhead without independent change rates.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team extracted 40 modules in one quarter, then clean builds improved only 12% because :core:common was api everywhere; the real win came from narrowing it and moving to KSP.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees or refuses wholesale, no measurement.
  • Hire: staged extraction with a pilot and baseline metrics.
  • Strong hire: ties extraction order to Wear reuse and conflict hot spots, limits api/impl, defines stop criteria.

questions.promptHtml: What does Kotlin internal actually guarantee across Gradle modules, and where does it leak?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates cite internal as the encapsulation tool without knowing it's a compile-time Kotlin rule.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "internal means visible within the same Kotlin module, which in Gradle terms is one source set compilation (main, plus test via association). Other Gradle modules can't reference it from Kotlin. But in bytecode it is public with a mangled name for members, so Java, reflection and some tooling can still reach it. It's a compiler guard, not a security boundary."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kotlin's "module" = a set of files compiled together (a Gradle source set). internal classes compile to public JVM classes (so same-package access from Java works); internal members get names like foo$moduleName to avoid accidental overrides/collisions. The test source set of the same Gradle module can see internal because it is associated with main compilation. Other Gradle modules can't, unless you use @PublishedApi internal for inline functions (exposes it to inline callers) or friend-module flags (avoid).

Practical use: data modules expose a repository interface and hide RetrofitService, DAOs, mappers as internal (the Android data module guidance explicitly suggests private/internal for data sources).

Gotchas: DI frameworks and kapt/KSP-generated code live in the same module, so internal classes are injectable inside the module. Hilt modules in :feature:impl can @Binds an internal impl to a public interface.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core:data
interface UserRepository { fun user(id: String): Flow<User> }

internal class DefaultUserRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val api: UserApi,        // internal too
) : UserRepository { /* ... */ }

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
internal interface DataModule {
    @Binds fun repo(impl: DefaultUserRepository): UserRepository
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Exposing an internal type in a public signature: compiler error ("exposes its internal type"), so people make it public instead of redesigning.
  • Assuming internal hides from Java callers.
  • @PublishedApi internal used casually, quietly widening the API.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can the app module instantiate an internal class from a feature? → No from Kotlin; the right pattern is a public factory or DI binding.
  2. Why do ViewModel test classes see internals? → Test compilation is associated with main.
  3. How to make internal boundaries stronger than the compiler? → Add Konsist/lint rules and avoid -Xfriend-paths-style tricks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions bytecode reality (public + mangling) and uses internal with DI bindings rather than public impl classes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reflection-based analytics tool found internal event classes via Java and a team treated them as API; a later rename broke an external consumer.

questions.promptHtml: Feature A needs to open a screen in feature B, but neither may depend on the other. How do you do it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common practical modularization question; reveals knowledge of mediator, api modules and deep links.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Options: (1) the app module owns the NavHost and wires destinations, with features exposing navigation callbacks (lambdas) rather than navigating themselves; (2) an api module holding the destination keys/routes that A depends on and B implements; (3) deep-link URIs as a string contract. I prefer a keys-in-api approach for typed args and callbacks for simple cases, passing ids not objects."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Android modularization guide describes a mediator (the module that owns the navigation graph, usually :app) forwarding data: navController.navigate("checkout/$bookId"), passing ids not objects so the destination loads from the shared data layer. It's a source-of-truth point too.

Patterns:

  • Callback hoisting: feature exposes fun CartRoute(onCheckout: (cartId: String) -> Unit); :app connects it. Zero dependencies, very testable.
  • Keys in api module: @Serializable data class CheckoutRoute(val cartId: String) in :feature:checkout:api. With Navigation 2.8+ type-safe routes or Navigation 3 keys (NiA docs: keys in api, entries in impl; check current Navigation 3 status, verify) feature A's impl references the key class only.
  • Deep link URIs: string-based, zero compile-time coupling, lose type safety; works for dynamic features not yet installed.
  • Central :navigation module holding all keys: simple but a change recompiles all dependents.
:feature:cart:impl --uses--> CheckoutRoute (in :feature:checkout:api)
:feature:checkout:impl registers composable<CheckoutRoute>
:app assembles NavHost { cartGraph(); checkoutGraph() }

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :feature:checkout:api
@Serializable data class CheckoutRoute(val cartId: String)

// :feature:cart:impl
fun NavGraphBuilder.cartScreen(onCheckout: (String) -> Unit) { /* ... */ }
// call site: navController.navigate(CheckoutRoute(cartId))   // key from api only

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing a serialized big object as navigation argument (process death, size limits, stale data).
  • Feature-to-feature implementation dependency "just for the route constant".
  • Registering destinations in the feature but forgetting :app must include its graph (runtime "destination not found").

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if B is a dynamic feature module? → Use a deep link or a string route resolved after install, since A can't reference its classes.
  2. How do you test the navigation wiring? → Compose navigation tests in :app verifying each key has a destination.
  3. Where do results flow back? → See the navigation chunk; prefer shared state in a data module or a result API, not direct references.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior compares callbacks vs api keys vs deep links with build and type-safety trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "navigation constants" object in :core:common grew to 200 routes and forced a rebuild of every feature on any route change.

questions.promptHtml: How do you structure shared UI and a design system in a modular app, and what are the traps?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shared UI is the first thing that becomes a dependency magnet.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A :core:designsystem with theme tokens and generic components (buttons, text fields) that know nothing about business models, and optionally a :core:ui for composites that use domain models. Features depend on them; they never depend on features. I keep component APIs primitive-typed, version them like a public library, and avoid putting feature-specific widgets in there."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Android guide lists a UI module as a common module, and notes centralized theming avoids a painful refactor on rebrand. Two-tier split:

:core:designsystem  (theme, typography, icons, Button, Card)  -> no domain deps
:core:ui            (NewsCard(NewsResource), UserAvatar(User)) -> depends on :core:model, designsystem
:feature:*          -> both

Reasons for the split: designsystem stays reusable (other apps, Wear) and recompiles rarely; :core:ui changes more often with models. Costs: one hot module on the path of every feature: a change to a Compose component's signature recompiles every UI module. Compose stability matters too (see A3 for compiler stability); modules from other layers are not "stable" unless configured (Compose compiler stability config file, verify version).

Resources: icons/strings/themes in designsystem use unique prefixes; with nonTransitiveRClass features reference R from their own module only.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core:designsystem
@Composable
fun AppButton(text: String, onClick: () -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) { /* ... */ }

// :core:ui (domain-aware)
@Composable
fun ProductCard(product: Product, onClick: (String) -> Unit) { /* uses AppButton */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Business strings or analytics calls inside designsystem components.
  • A single :ui module with 400 composables recompiled on every change.
  • Components with many nullable params to serve each feature, becoming unmaintainable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Preview and screenshot tests? → Keep a catalog/sample in the designsystem module for fast iteration.
  2. How to evolve a component API safely? → Deprecate with @Deprecated(ReplaceWith), migrate gradually, avoid breaking all features in one PR.
  3. Theming per brand/white label? → Theme tokens injected via CompositionLocal and swapped in :app flavors.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior separates domain-free and domain-aware layers and reasons about change frequency and recompilation fan-out.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rebrand touching one theme file was a 2-day task thanks to centralized tokens; in another app with hard-coded colors it was a quarter.
