Relevant build files:

// :feature:cart/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":feature:recommendations"))   // show strip
    api(project(":core:network"))
}
// :feature:recommendations/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":feature:cart"))              // reuse CartItemRow, AddToCart action
}

A teammate proposes a fix: move CartItemRow and AddToCart into :core:common.
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong with the build files, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts the move to :core:common ("it compiles") or deletes one dependency and copy-pastes the code. Doesn't notice api(project(":core:network")) or ask which direction should exist.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who owns each feature? What exactly does Recommendations need from Cart (UI row, action, data)? Is Recommendations a sibling or a sub-part of Cart? Do other features also want the strip?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the PR or stub the strip behind a placeholder so main is green.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a UI component and a use-case are shared and should live below both, (b) Recommendations should be a leaf that exposes a composable with callbacks and Cart hosts it, (c) the two features are really one feature.
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep which symbols recommendations imports from cart; ./gradlew :feature:cart:dependencies --configuration debugCompileClasspath.
  5. Root cause: Sibling features depend on each other; direction was never set. Also the stray api(project(":core:network")) leaks network types to every consumer of cart.
  6. Fix: Short-term: Recommendations exposes RecommendationsStrip(onAddToCart: (String) -> Unit) and takes item data via its own repository; Cart depends on Recommendations (one-way), Cart handles add-to-cart. Shared row composable moves to :core:ui only if truly generic. Long-term: if more features want it, :feature:recommendations:api.
  7. Prevention: Konsist/Gradle check that no :feature:* depends on :feature:* except :api; PR template question "which direction?".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not dumping into :core:common; not duplicating the row; not weakening checks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Both features truly need each other's data? → Extract a shared data module they both depend on; or a mediator at :app.
  • Can't change ownership boundaries this sprint? → Temporarily merge the code into Cart as a package, extract later.
  • api vs implementation for network? → implementation, unless Retrofit types appear in public signatures.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" :core:common move turned into a 300-file module that every change rebuilt; the team spent a month untangling it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: moves code to common to compile.
  • Hire: breaks the cycle by choosing a direction and callback.
  • Strong hire: also catches the api leak and adds automated enforcement.

questions.promptHtml: How fine-grained should modules be? What are the signals that you have too many or too few?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Judgement question; there is no formula, so interviewers look for a decision framework.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Cut on change boundaries: things that change together stay together (high cohesion), things that change at different rates or by different teams split. Too fine: lots of one-file modules, sync and config time growing, constant cross-module PRs. Too coarse: modules over tens of thousands of lines, everyone editing the same one, no incremental benefit."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The Android guide names three pitfalls: too fine-grained (overhead in build complexity and boilerplate), too coarse (another monolith), too complex (small project). The tip: if two modules heavily rely on each other's knowledge they probably are one system; if two parts of a module rarely interact, split them.

Signals table:

Signal Too fine Too coarse
PR shape every feature change touches 3+ modules many devs conflict in one module
Build configuration time grows with project count one module is on every critical path
Boilerplate module files longer than code internal types leak because no boundary
Ownership one owner for 15 modules no clear owner

Costs per module (rough, measure yourself): configuration time for each project, a build.gradle.kts, a manifest/namespace, possible Hilt/KSP task set, IDE indexing, and cognitive load. Benefits: parallelism (modules with no dependency between them can compile in parallel with org.gradle.parallel=true), build cache hit granularity, visibility control.

Practical heuristic: start with core + a feature per top-level destination; split a feature further only when a team boundary or build hot spot appears.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// pragmatic: one module per feature, packages inside by layer
:feature:checkout
  └ ui/ domain/ data/   // internal packages; split data out only if reused elsewhere

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Module per layer per feature (3 x N modules) at a 5-person team.
  • Never splitting because "it works" until builds exceed ten minutes.
  • Counting modules rather than measuring cache hit rate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When do you split a feature into api/impl? → Once another feature needs to reference it.
  2. Does module count hurt config time? → Yes, roughly linear in projects; configuration cache mitigates (see build chunk).
  3. How do you merge modules back? → Move code, delete module, update deps; cheap when boundaries were clean.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior frames it as change-rate cohesion and monitors cost metrics, accepting reversibility.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team with 310 modules for 20 engineers saw 70 s configuration without the configuration cache and consolidated leaf modules by 40%.

questions.promptHtml: What are convention plugins, why do multi-module Android projects need them, and why prefer build-logic over buildSrc?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who maintained 50+ modules from those who copy-paste Gradle files.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A convention plugin is a Gradle plugin in the repo that encodes the standard configuration (Android library setup, Kotlin options, Compose, Hilt, test deps) so each module applies one plugin id instead of repeating 40 lines. I put them in an included build build-logic, not buildSrc, because changing buildSrc invalidates build-script classpath for the whole build and can ruin caching; an included build is more targeted and lets plugins use the version catalog."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problem: 80 modules x copy-pasted compileSdk, jvmTarget, lint options, test deps drift apart, and a version bump is an 80-file change (the Android guide: use version catalogs plus convention plugins for consistent configuration).

Mechanism: a build-logic included build (pluginManagement { includeBuild("build-logic") }) with plugins registered via gradlePlugin { plugins { register(...) } }, written in Kotlin against com.android.build.api.dsl.* types (CommonExtension, LibraryExtension). Modules do plugins { id("app.android.feature") }. Version catalog accessed from build-logic via a catalog import or file.

build-logic/convention/src/main/kotlin/
  AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin.kt
  AndroidFeatureConventionPlugin.kt   (applies library + compose + hilt + common deps)

buildSrc vs included build: both are compiled before the main build. buildSrc is on the classpath of all build scripts, so any edit invalidates every script's compilation and many task inputs; included builds scope better and can be split. Gradle's guidance leans to included builds (verify against current Gradle docs for your version).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        pluginManager.apply("com.android.library")
        pluginManager.apply("org.jetbrains.kotlin.android")
        extensions.configure<LibraryExtension> {
            compileSdk = 35
            defaultConfig.minSdk = 24
            compileOptions { sourceCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17; targetCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17 }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Convention plugin that applies everything (Hilt, Compose) to modules that don't need it, slowing builds.
  • Reading project properties lazily wrong, causing configuration-cache problems.
  • Using subprojects {}/allprojects {} blocks in root build (couples projects, hurts configuration avoidance).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Precompiled script plugins vs class plugins? → Script plugins (*.gradle.kts in build-logic) are quicker to write; class plugins give typed control; both are fine.
  2. How do you share the version catalog? → Include the catalog file in build-logic's settings, or read via VersionCatalogsExtension in the plugin.
  3. How do you stay config-cache compatible? → No Project access at execution time, use providers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior can explain invalidation difference, config avoidance and keeps plugins composable (library, feature, compose, hilt separate).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A single buildSrc edit to bump a dependency forced a full rebuild for every developer and CI shard; after moving to build-logic + catalog, version bumps were a one-line catalog change.

questions.promptHtml: How should a data module be designed so features can use it without coupling to its internals?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests encapsulation at the data boundary in a modular setting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "One data module per domain (orders, user, catalog), exposing a repository interface plus its public models, and hiding data sources, DTOs, DAOs and mappers behind internal. Features inject the repository, never a Retrofit service or DAO. Models crossing the boundary are domain models, not DTOs/entities."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the Android guide, a data module's three responsibilities: encapsulate a domain's data and business logic; expose the repository as its external API; hide data sources.

:core:data-orders (public)       internal
  OrdersRepository  ---------->  OrdersApi (Retrofit), OrdersDao, OrderDto, OrderEntity, mappers
  Order (model)

Choices:

  • Models in the same module (Order) vs a shared :core:model: put them in :core:model only when multiple data modules/features need them; otherwise keep next to the repo to limit fan-out (every model change recompiles dependents of :core:model).
  • api vs implementation on Room/Retrofit inside the data module: implementation, so consumers can't use them.
  • Cross-domain needs: data module A depends on B's repository, not B's data sources.

Testing: expose a testFixtures/fake implementation (e.g. FakeOrdersRepository) from a test module so features test without the real thing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// public
interface OrdersRepository {
    fun observeOrders(): Flow<List<Order>>
    suspend fun refresh(): Result<Unit>
}
// hidden
internal class OrdersRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val api: OrdersApi, private val dao: OrdersDao,
) : OrdersRepository { /* ... */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Exposing DTOs because mapping "seems like boilerplate", so a backend field rename ripples to all UI.
  • One giant :core:data for the entire app, a hot module for every feature.
  • Repositories depending on feature modules (upward dependency).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do mappers live? → Inside the data module, internal.
  2. Single :core:data vs per-domain? → Per-domain once teams/entities diverge; single is fine small.
  3. How do you swap implementations per environment? → Impl module or DI binding chosen in :app.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior ties visibility to change fan-out and designs fakes as part of the module contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A backend rename of price to amount hit 14 screens when DTOs leaked; after the boundary fix it hit one mapper.

questions.contextHtml: A 5-year-old app: one :app module, ~420k LOC, 2.5M DAU, weekly releases, crash-free sessions 99.6%. 14 engineers across 4 squads, feature code interleaved with util, base and common packages, plenty of singletons and a god AppDatabase. Incremental build is 3 min 20 s. Leadership allows "no feature freeze, no drop in crash-free rate". You must propose and run the migration to modules over two quarters.
questions.promptHtml: What is your step-by-step plan, and how do you keep releases safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Create modules and move classes until it compiles." No ordering, no safety nets, no definition of done, and a long-lived branch that rots.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which squads own which areas (extraction follows ownership)? What are the worst build hot spots (build scan)? Is DI in place (Hilt/Dagger/none)? Test coverage on the areas I'd move? Any dynamic-delivery or multi-app goals that change priorities?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing is broken; I'd lock in a baseline (build scan, crash-free, startup time) and agree on stop-the-line metrics so any extraction PR that regresses them is reverted.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the biggest risk is hidden coupling through singletons/Application statics, (b) resource and manifest merging surprises, (c) R8/ProGuard rules and DI bindings lost when code moves, (d) long-lived branches.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dependency analysis of imports (a script or Konsist) to produce a "who imports whom" matrix; compile after each move; release-build smoke test with R8 on; startup benchmarks.
  5. Root cause: Absent boundaries, so anything can use anything.
  6. Fix (plan):
    • Phase 0: version catalog, convention plugins, module template, CI check scripts. No code moves.
    • Phase 1: leaves first: :core:model, :core:designsystem, :core:network, :core:database, utilities. Mechanical moves, small PRs, trunk-based, merged daily.
    • Phase 2: one pilot feature, owned by one squad, extracted behind its existing public entry points, after introducing interfaces for what it needs from the rest of the monolith (strangler: define the seam in :app first, then move).
    • Phase 3: remaining features by squad, ordered by build pain, replacing cross-feature calls with navigation callbacks or api modules.
    • Phase 4: shrink :app to composition root; enforce direction with checks. Safety: every PR is move-only plus visibility change; release with staged rollout (1% to 10% to 50%); compare crash and ANR per version in Crashlytics/Vitals.
  7. Prevention: A dependency-direction check in CI; CODEOWNERS per module; a "no new code in :app" rule after phase 3.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No long-lived migration branch, no big-bang rename, no api/impl everywhere on day one, no mixed refactoring of logic during moves.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A feature is entangled with a god singleton? → Introduce an interface in a lower module, make the singleton implement it, move the consumer first, then split the singleton.
  • Release-only crash after extraction? → Check consumer ProGuard rules and merged manifest first (see the R8 scenario).
  • A squad refuses the pilot? → Pick the squad with the worst merge-conflict data; let metrics persuade.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's phase 2 stalled for weeks on Application-level statics; adding a thin AppContext interface in :core unblocked six extractions in a sprint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang or "move until it compiles".
  • Hire: leaf-first, incremental, feature pilot, staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: strangler seams, metrics gates, ownership-driven order, enforcement after migration.

questions.promptHtml: How do Play Feature Delivery dynamic feature modules differ from ordinary feature modules, and what architectural constraints do they impose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know "feature module" has two meanings and the limits of on-demand code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A dynamic feature module is a separate split APK delivered by Play: at install, conditionally, or on demand. It depends on the base module (not vice versa), so the base can't reference its classes at compile time. That forces loose coupling: reflection/ServiceLoader, deep links or interfaces from the base, SplitCompat, and care with DI, exports, R8 and offline users."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the Play docs: modules use the com.android.dynamic-feature plugin; the base module lists them in android.dynamicFeatures; the feature module depends on the base via implementation(project(":app")). Omit signing, minifyEnabled, version code in the feature (inherited from base); extra ProGuard rules are allowed per feature but apply to the whole app. Delivery options: install-time (default), on-demand, conditional (device features, locale, min API), instant.

Constraints:

  • Direction is inverted: dynamic feature to app. So the base needs an abstraction (interface or deep link) to launch it, and a feature module must be loaded before its code is touched. Enable SplitCompat for on-demand code and resources.
  • Docs: installing 50+ modules on one device may cause performance issues; limit removable install-time modules to 10 or fewer; on-demand needs API 21+ (fusing for older).
  • Activities in a dynamic feature shouldn't be android:exported="true" since the device may not have downloaded it.
  • Dependency injection: Hilt's support for DFMs is limited (Hilt generates one component graph in the app; DFM code needs entry points or Dagger component dependencies; verify current Hilt docs).
  • If a module has no code, set android:hasCode="false" and handle the base manifest override.
:app (base)  <--implementation(project(":app"))-- :feature:ar (dynamic)
   |  no compile-time reference to :feature:ar
   +-- SplitInstallManager.startInstall("ar") -> then launch via className / deep link

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// base module: ask for the module, then start via class name (no compile dep)
val request = SplitInstallRequest.newBuilder().addModule("ar").build()
splitInstallManager.startInstall(request).addOnSuccessListener {
    startActivity(Intent().setClassName(packageName, "com.example.ar.ArActivity"))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using DFMs "to speed up builds" instead of regular modules; they add delivery complexity.
  • No offline/failed-install UX; feature absent on first launch.
  • Missing SplitCompat so resources of a just-installed module aren't visible until restart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a DFM worth it? → Large, rarely used features (e.g. an AR or KYC flow used by 10% of users) where install size matters.
  2. How do you test? → bundletool/--apks local install, internal app sharing, because debug APK installs fuse features.
  3. Impact on crash reporting? → Class names in stack traces exist, but ClassNotFound/missing-split crashes need monitoring per module.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the inverted dependency, SplitCompat, export rules, limits, and that regular modules solve build problems.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An on-demand KYC module used reflection to launch; an R8 rule missing the class name caused ClassNotFoundException only in release.

questions.contextHtml:
After extracting :feature:profile, Android Studio shows red R.string.title in :feature:orders code (compiles previously). Someone "fixes" it with android.nonTransitiveRClass=false in gradle.properties. A week later QA reports Orders shows "Profile" as its screen title. Both modules define <string name="title">. Snippet:

<!-- :feature:orders/res/values/strings.xml -->
<string name="title">Orders</string>
<!-- :feature:profile/res/values/strings.xml -->
<string name="title">Profile</string>
// :feature:orders
Text(stringResource(R.string.title))   // shows "Profile" in the final app

Modules are merged by dependency priority; :app depends on both.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bug, why the "fix" caused it, and the right solution.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames Compose or caching; renames one string without understanding resource merging or the R class setting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which AGP version and what was the nonTransitiveRClass setting (AGP 8.0 and later default non-transitive, verify for your version)? Do both modules use the same resource name? Is it only in the merged app or also in module previews?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the property flip; ship a hotfix renaming Orders' string.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) name collision resolved by manifest merger-like resource priority (app, then dependencies in order), (b) transitive R class made R.string.title resolve to the other module's ID, (c) stale build.
  4. How I'd verify each: Print R.string.title ids in each module; inspect APK with APK Analyzer / ./gradlew :app:mergeDebugResources output; check lint "duplicate resource".
  5. Root cause: Library resources merge into one namespace in the final APK; same name means the higher-priority module wins. With non-transitive R, each module's R holds only its own resources, so the original error was legit: Orders was referencing a resource it never declared (it had been accidentally relying on a transitive one). Flipping to transitive hid that and made collisions silent.
  6. Fix: Keep non-transitive R. Give Orders its own string with a module prefix (orders_title) and reference its own R; use resourcePrefix = "orders_" in the module's Android block so lint enforces it. Short-term: hotfix rename.
  7. Prevention: resourcePrefix in the convention plugin; lint check for missing prefix; keep strings in the module that uses them; shared strings only in designsystem/core.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not re-enabling transitive R (bigger R classes, slower builds, hidden dependencies); not sharing a generic title string across modules.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Overlay intended (white label)? → Use flavor source sets in :app for overrides deliberately.
  • Drawable named same in two modules? → Same merge rule; prefix.
  • Compose-only modules? → Strings and drawables still collide via resource IDs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A white-label app's brand color silently came from the wrong module because of merge priority; the fix was resourcePrefix and a lint rule.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: renames only the symptom.
  • Hire: explains merge priority and non-transitive R.
  • Strong hire: adds prefix enforcement and distinguishes intended overlays.

questions.promptHtml: Modules exist, but how do you stop the architecture from eroding over 3 years?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Architecture without enforcement decays; seniors automate.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I layer enforcement: Gradle structure itself (modules, implementation, internal), automated checks on the module graph in CI (feature modules can't depend on each other, core can't depend on features), Konsist or lint rules for code-level rules, and the dependency-analysis plugin for unused or leaked api. Plus CODEOWNERS and a short architecture decision record so the rules have reasons."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers, cheapest first:

  1. Compile-time: absent dependency means no access; internal/private; implementation instead of api.
  2. Module graph check: a Gradle task walking project.configurations to assert forbidden edges (e.g. any :feature:* project dependency on another :feature:* that isn't :api). Fails CI on violation.
  3. Code rules: Konsist (Kotlin architecture tests, verify current API) such as "classes in ..ui.. must not import ..data..", ViewModels named *ViewModel extend ViewModel; custom Android Lint detectors for project-specific bans.
  4. Dependency analysis plugin (Autonomous Autonomy / dependency-analysis-gradle-plugin): finds unused deps, api that should be implementation.
  5. Human: CODEOWNERS, module READMEs, review checklist.
PR -> Gradle graph check -> Konsist tests -> lint -> dependency analysis -> merge

Trade-off: strict rules block urgent fixes; have an explicit exception mechanism (allowlist with owner and expiry).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// root build.gradle.kts: illustrative graph assertion
tasks.register("checkModuleRules") {
    doLast {
        rootProject.subprojects.forEach { p ->
            if (p.path.startsWith(":feature:") && !p.path.endsWith(":api")) {
                val bad = p.configurations.flatMap { c -> c.dependencies.withType<ProjectDependency>() }
                    .map { it.path }.filter { it.startsWith(":feature:") && !it.endsWith(":api") }
                check(bad.isEmpty()) { "${p.path} depends on features: $bad" }
            }
        }
    }
}

(Accessing dependencyProject/configurations at execution time is not configuration-cache friendly; do it at configuration or use a plugin. Verify for your Gradle.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Rules only in a wiki page.
  • Tests that are slow or flaky so people bypass them.
  • Hard rules without an allowlist, creating a revolt.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not only code review? → Humans miss transitive and mechanical violations.
  2. How do you introduce rules on a violating codebase? → Baseline existing violations, fail on new ones, burn the baseline down.
  3. Konsist vs ArchUnit? → ArchUnit works on bytecode (JVM); Konsist on Kotlin source so it sees Kotlin-specific constructs (verify details).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior has a multi-layer, baseline-friendly approach and cost-aware exceptions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature importing another feature's internal via reflection slipped through review for a year; a graph check plus baseline found 23 violations to fix incrementally.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 8.14 moves the "Scan to pay" flow (used by ~6% of 1.8M DAU) into an on-demand dynamic feature to cut a 78 MB APK. Within 24 h: Crashlytics shows ClassNotFoundException: com.shop.scan.ScanActivity at 0.4% of sessions, concentrated on Android 7-8 and low-storage devices; Play Console install-failure rate for the module is 3%. Also Resources$NotFoundException after successful installs on some devices. Overall crash-free sessions fell from 99.5% to 99.1%. Activity code:

splitInstallManager.startInstall(request)
    .addOnSuccessListener { startActivity(Intent(this, ScanActivity::class.java)) }

ScanActivity is referenced directly in the base through a compileOnly shim.
questions.promptHtml: Triage and fix this incident, then say what you'd change in the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add try/catch around startActivity" and move on; doesn't distinguish install failures, SplitCompat, and launch-by-class.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is SplitCompat installed in Application and activities? What does the success listener do (module installed vs state INSTALLED)? Are users offline or low on storage? Which Play Core/feature-delivery library version? Did we enable fusing/min API 21?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config kill switch to hide Scan entry or fall back to a base-module scanner; halt staged rollout; consider hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) missing SplitCompat so new code/resources not visible until restart, (b) launching via a class reference/Intent before module active, (c) install failures (storage, network, ACTIVE_SESSIONS_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) not handled, (d) R8 removed or renamed a class (it appears only in release).
  4. How I'd verify each: Check install-state listener codes; reproduce with bundletool --local-testing and internal app sharing; Play Console feature install stats; inspect the mapping file; test on API 24 low storage emulator.
  5. Root cause: Start-up relied on class reference after install without SplitCompat and without robust state handling; failures treated as success path only.
  6. Fix: Short-term: kill switch, fix SplitCompat (SplitCompatApplication or SplitCompat.install), launch via Intent().setClassName(...) after confirming SplitInstallSessionStatus.INSTALLED, show error/retry UI for failure codes, request module again only if isInstalled. Long-term: abstraction in base (ScannerLauncher interface via ServiceLoader or deep link) with a fallback screen, and track install funnel metrics.
  7. Prevention: CI test on bundletool-generated APK set; a "feature not installed" test; keep rules for dynamic classes; alerts on install failure rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not shipping DFM for 6% users if size win is small; not making ScanActivity exported; not bundling as install-time removable for 20 modules.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users with no network at checkout? → Install-time delivery or fallback to base scanning; DFM is a bad fit for critical paths.
  • Is the 78 MB reduction real? → Measure per-split download size in Play Console; compare with R8/resource shrinking first.
  • Does Hilt work inside the DFM? → Limited; use entry points (verify current docs).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team moved a core flow to on-demand delivery, discovered airplane-mode and Play-store-not-ready edge cases, and later made it install-time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: catches the exception.
  • Hire: SplitCompat, install states, kill switch.
  • Strong hire: questions the decision, adds funnel metrics, abstraction with fallback.

questions.promptHtml: How do you share fakes and test data across modules without creating dependency cycles or shipping them in production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Test infrastructure is a common casualty of modularization; weak designs duplicate fakes everywhere.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I give each api/data module a matching fake or a java-test-fixtures source set, or a dedicated :core:testing module consumed only through testImplementation/androidTestImplementation. Fakes implement the same contract as the production implementation, so features test against them and never against real network or DB."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Options:

Option Pros Cons
Duplicate fakes in each module no coupling drift, wasteful
:core:testing module (test dispatchers, rules, builders) simple becomes a dumping ground; must not depend on features
java-test-fixtures plugin (testFixtures source set per module) fakes live with their contract, versioned together Android library support exists in AGP (opt-in android.testFixtures.enable/testFixtures { enable = true }, verify AGP version)
:module:fake implementation module selected by DI in debug/test builds extra modules

Rules: shared test code depends on api modules only; production code never depends on it; use testImplementation, and Android guide's test module guidance. Contract tests: a reusable abstract test suite run against both fake and real implementation ensures fakes don't drift.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core:data-orders testFixtures
class FakeOrdersRepository : OrdersRepository {
    private val orders = MutableStateFlow<List<Order>>(emptyList())
    override fun observeOrders(): Flow<List<Order>> = orders
    override suspend fun refresh(): Result<Unit> = Result.success(Unit)
    fun emit(list: List<Order>) { orders.value = list }
}
// :feature:orders build
// testImplementation(testFixtures(project(":core:data-orders")))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mocks everywhere with Mockito, tying tests to implementation details.
  • :core:testing depending on production features, creating cycles.
  • Fakes that always succeed, hiding error paths.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do TestDispatcher rules go? → :core:testing, with no Android feature deps.
  2. How do you keep a fake honest? → A shared contract test run against both.
  3. Hilt tests replacing bindings? → @TestInstallIn with the fake module (see the Hilt chunk).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs fakes as part of module contracts and prevents test code from leaking into production.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Divergent copies of FakeUserRepository in 11 modules made a User model change a 30-file test fix.

questions.contextHtml: Checkout (:feature:checkout) needs the address the user selected in Profile (:feature:profile), and must refresh when the user edits it. Three proposals in design review: (A) checkout depends on profile implementation and calls ProfileViewModel; (B) an event bus (SharedFlow in :core:common) where profile emits AddressChanged; (C) a shared AddressRepository in a data module with a Flow<Address>. Two squads own the features; ~1.2M checkouts/week, address staleness bugs already cost 0.8% of orders (wrong address).
questions.promptHtml: Which would you choose and why? What are the failure modes of each?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks the quickest (A or B) without discussing ownership, source of truth, process death or ordering.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where is the address truly stored (server, local)? Who may edit it? Does checkout need the latest only or history? What happens if profile is not on the back stack? Offline behavior?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; but I'd add a re-fetch at checkout entry to stop the stale-address bug now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Stale data arises from multiple owners of the same truth; the right fix moves ownership to a data layer.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce: edit address, navigate back, check; trace where checkout reads it; test process death.
  5. Root cause: Two features keep separate copies of the same fact, synchronized (or not) by navigation timing.
  6. Fix: (C). Address lives behind AddressRepository in a data module both depend on, observing a single source of truth (local DB or cache backed by network). Features pass at most an id through navigation. (A) creates feature-to-feature coupling and ViewModel sharing across modules; (B) hides dependencies, loses events when no collector is active, has no replay/state semantics, and fails on process death.
  7. Prevention: Rule: "state shared across features lives in a data module, exposed as Flow"; test with a fake repository emitting updates.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: (C) costs a shared module and contract negotiation between squads (owner: the profile squad, consumers read-only). I wouldn't add an event bus for state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Checkout must work if the address changes mid-payment? → Snapshot the address at order creation and send its id/version.
  • Both teams want to write? → Repository exposes explicit update API; conflict handled server-side with versions.
  • Need an ephemeral signal (e.g. "address saved" toast)? → A navigation result or one-off effect in the editing feature, not a global bus.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A global event bus was used for cross-feature state; a screen that opened after the event never received it and the team spent weeks adding sticky events before moving to repository flows.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses A or B.
  • Hire: chooses C with reasoning on source of truth.
  • Strong hire: addresses snapshot semantics, ownership and one-off signals separately.

questions.contextHtml: :core:common is now 1,900 files across 14 packages (strings utils, UserSession, retrofit interceptors, five unrelated enums, analytics events, three feature-specific mappers). All 45 modules depend on it with api. Last month a one-line change to a date formatter forced all 45 modules to recompile and relaunched 2,300 unit tests (CI +22 min). A second incident: a feature team's enum change in common broke another team's feature at runtime (serialization name). Three squads own different parts; no one owns common.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review: what happened, and how do you decompose common and prevent regrowth?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Split it into :core:utils and :core:common2". Doesn't tackle api, ownership, or dependencies by consumers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the import graph per package (who uses what)? Which parts are used by only one module? Are there any cycles inside? What's the cost per recompile in minutes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Change api(project(":core:common")) to implementation where possible (compile errors reveal real uses), freeze additions to common through CODEOWNERS.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) most of common is used by 1-2 modules and belongs there, (b) a small set (date, result types) is truly shared, (c) UserSession and interceptors are really data/network concerns.
  4. How I'd verify each: Import matrix by package (script/Konsist), dependency-analysis plugin report, build scan task graph.
  5. Root cause: No ownership plus "if in doubt, put it in common" and api exposure made everything a build-wide dependency.
  6. Fix: Move code to the single consumer; extract cohesive modules (:core:datetime, :core:network, :core:analytics, :core:session); keep a tiny :core:common for truly generic pure-Kotlin utilities; mark implementation; assign owners. Shared enum with serialization names goes to its owning data module with tests.
  7. Prevention: CODEOWNERS for every module, size budget alert on :core:common (files, dependents), "no feature code in core" lint, review checklist question "who else needs this?".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big-bang split (do it per package, PR per move); not renaming and leaving everything inside; not blaming individuals.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A package is used by 30 modules but changes weekly? → Split by change rate; stable core vs hot parts.
  • Squads disagree on ownership? → Default owner is the squad with most commits, and the module doc lists a contact.
  • Is deleting duplicate utils worth it? → Only when it removes a dependency edge.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After untangling a 1,500-file common module, the median PR touched 2 modules instead of 9 and CI incremental test time dropped by about a third.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: splits arbitrarily.
  • Hire: moves to consumers, uses implementation, adds ownership.
  • Strong hire: data-driven, baseline guard, CODEOWNERS and size budgets.

questions.contextHtml:
You extracted :core:network and :feature:feed. Debug builds and instrumented tests pass. Release 4.2 goes to 5% staged rollout; 11 minutes later Crashlytics shows 3.1% of sessions crash on launch:

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Unable to create converter for class com.app.network.dto.FeedDto
Caused by: kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException: Serializer for class 'FeedDto' is not found.

and elsewhere NoSuchMethodException: com.app.feed.FeedViewModel.<init>. Previously ProGuard keep rules lived in :app/proguard-rules.pro and referenced old package names. Distractors: a Retrofit bump the same week, and a server deploy that morning.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through diagnosis, mitigation and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the server deploy or Retrofit and rolls those back; doesn't test a minified build.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is minifyEnabled/R8 on only in release? Do library modules ship consumer rules? Did package names change in the move? Is it a launch crash for all or specific devices?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt rollout; roll back to previous version (staged 5% limits exposure); if a hotfix is quick, add keep rules.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) keep rules referencing old packages no longer match moved classes, (b) library modules need consumerProguardFiles for their own reflection/serialization usage, (c) serializer generated class stripped, (d) Retrofit bump (red herring), (e) server (red herring: crash is client-side stack).
  4. How I'd verify each: Build the release variant locally and run; compare mapping.txt, usage.txt and configuration.txt (-printconfiguration); retrace the stack; diff old/new keep rules.
  5. Root cause: R8 runs on the whole app; rules belong with the code that needs them. After the move, :app rules no longer matched, and library modules had no consumer rules, so R8 removed/renamed classes used reflectively.
  6. Fix: Short-term: update rules for new packages. Long-term: each library module declares consumerProguardFiles("consumer-rules.pro") with minimal rules for what it needs (e.g. keep serializable DTO companions); prefer libraries that bundle their own rules; app-level rules only for app code.
  7. Prevention: CI builds a minified release APK and runs smoke/instrumented tests against it (an androidTest on release-like variant or a benchmark build type); canary rollouts; mapping upload.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not broad -keep class com.app.** { *; } (kills shrinking win); not disabling R8; not relying on debug tests.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Do library modules run R8 themselves? → No, R8 runs for the app module over all dependencies (library minify is generally not recommended); consumer rules flow to the app.
  • Dynamic feature module rules? → Per-feature ProGuard files merge app-wide (Play docs).
  • What if a third-party lib lacks rules? → Add narrowly scoped rules, upstream an issue.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team moved DTOs into a new module and an unrelated -keep pattern no longer matched; a minified smoke test in CI became mandatory after.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: investigates server/Retrofit.
  • Hire: identifies rules and tests release build.
  • Strong hire: consumer rules per module, minified CI test, narrow keep rules.

questions.promptHtml: Which modules should be pure Kotlin/JVM instead of Android libraries, and what does that buy you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests build-cost awareness and readiness for KMP/shared code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Anything with no Android framework dependency (domain models, use cases, business rules, mappers) can be a pure Kotlin/JVM module. They compile faster (no AAR packaging, no resource processing or manifest merge), run unit tests on the JVM instantly, and are one step from becoming Kotlin Multiplatform common code. The Android guide says to prefer Kotlin/Java modules where possible."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three module kinds (Android guide): app, Android library (AAR with resources/manifest), Kotlin/Java library (plain JAR). Android library modules incur extra tasks (manifest merge, resource compile/link, AAR packaging, R class generation). A pure module uses kotlin("jvm") or org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm plugin.

Candidates: :core:model, :core:domain, validators, mappers, algorithms. Not candidates: anything touching Context, Parcelable (use @Parcelize only if Android), Compose, Room (use KMP Room if multiplatform).

Gotcha: Android library depending on a JVM module is fine; JVM module depending on Android modules is impossible. So keep the direction: Android to pure. Kotlin/JVM modules and java.time on older minSdk need desugaring in the consuming app (core library desugaring) — verify.

KMP path: convert JVM module to kotlin("multiplatform") with androidTarget()/jvm() and commonMain (see the KMP chunk), mostly a build-file change if you avoided JDK-only APIs (e.g. java.util.UUID).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core:domain/build.gradle.kts
plugins { kotlin("jvm") }
dependencies {
    api(project(":core:model"))
    implementation(libs.kotlinx.coroutines.core)
    testImplementation(libs.junit)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using android.util.Log or Parcelable in domain code and having to keep it Android.
  • Making everything pure and then needing Android types, adding wrappers.
  • Different JVM target between modules.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep Android types out? → Interfaces (e.g. Logger, Clock) injected from Android modules.
  2. DI in pure modules? → Constructor injection with javax.inject annotations (no Android), bound in Hilt modules elsewhere.
  3. Test speed benefit? → JVM tests avoid Robolectric/emulator.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior quantifies the build task savings conceptually and sees pure modules as an enforcement of "no Android in domain".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving pricing rules to a pure module let 600 tests run in 4 s instead of 90 s under Robolectric, and later enabled sharing with the iOS app.

questions.contextHtml: Greenfield ride-hailing app: rider app first, driver app in 9 months, ~25 engineers by year 2 in 5 squads (Booking, Payments, Trip, Safety, Growth). Requirements are vague: "needs to ship in 4 months, then scale". Payments will use two providers by region; Maps SDK may be swapped; Safety must be able to release independent hotfixes quickly. Currently 6 engineers.
questions.promptHtml: Design the module structure and describe how it evolves.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Draws 40 modules immediately or a single module with no evolution path; doesn't separate rider/driver reuse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's shared between rider and driver (maps, auth, trip model)? Is the driver app confirmed? KMP/iOS shared code? Minimum devices and API level? Any regulatory isolation (payments, PCI)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; I'd propose a day-1 minimal setup (version catalog, convention plugins) to avoid migration pain.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Reuse boundary (rider vs driver) is the main structural force; payments and maps are swappable, so api/impl applies there; the rest stays coarse until teams grow.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype dependency diagram with squad leads, check for forced cross-squad edges, measure build after the first feature.
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix (design):
    • Day 1 (6 engineers): :app-rider, :core:designsystem, :core:model, :core:network, :core:data, :feature:booking, :feature:trip, :feature:payments (+ :payments:api and :payments:impl:providerA), :maps:api + :maps:impl:google.
    • Month 9: add :app-driver, reuse core modules; promote driver-only features; extract :feature:trip shared parts into :trip:api.
    • Year 2: split features by squad, add :safety:api for Trip to trigger safety flows; convention plugins, graph checks, CODEOWNERS; consider dynamic delivery only for large, rare features. Dependency direction: apps to features to api modules and core; impls only in app modules.
  7. Prevention: ADR documenting rules, graph check in CI, module template generator.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No module per screen, no api/impl for everything on day one, no premature DFM; keep reversibility.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Safety needs independent release? → Isolated module plus feature flags/remote kill switch; true independent release would need separate app or DFM (trade-offs).
  • Add iOS code sharing? → Make model/domain/data pure Kotlin so KMP conversion is incremental.
  • Team grows to 50? → More vertical slices, platform team owning build-logic and core.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A greenfield team that started with 60 modules for 8 engineers spent months on cross-module friction and merged back to 12; a staged design avoided that.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-or-nothing structure.
  • Hire: sensible core/feature split with swappable api/impl for payments and maps.
  • Strong hire: stages growth, ties structure to reuse and ownership, includes enforcement and reversibility.

questions.promptHtml: What are the most common modularization anti-patterns you've seen, and how do you recognize each one early?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A summary of experience: do you know how modularization fails in practice?

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Layer-only modules (:data, :domain, :ui giants), a dumping-ground common, module per class, api everywhere, feature-to-feature dependencies, impl leaking into consumers, hidden dependencies through service locators or static singletons, and modules with no owner. Each shows up as one signal: PRs touching many modules, recompiling everything, or imports crossing boundaries."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Anti-pattern Symptom Fix
Horizontal layer modules only every feature touches 3 modules, no team isolation vertical feature slices, layers as packages inside
God common/core builds rebuild everything, no owner split by cohesion, CODEOWNERS
Module per class/screen config time up, boilerplate consolidate by change rate
api everywhere one leaf change rebuilds all implementation default, dependency analysis
Feature-to-feature implementation cycles, rebuild fan-out api modules, callbacks, mediator
Hidden coupling via static locator modules "independent" yet fail at runtime constructor injection, DI in app
api module with heavy deps consumers pull Retrofit/Room keep api module dependency-free
Dynamic feature used for build speed delivery complexity regular module
Modules without enforcement erosion in 6-12 months graph checks, Konsist

Underlying principle: a module boundary is only valuable if it reflects a real difference in ownership, change rate, reuse or delivery. If you cannot name which of those a boundary serves, it is overhead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// anti-pattern: service locator hides a cross-module dependency
object ServiceLocator { lateinit var analytics: Analytics }   // any module can call; nothing declared

// better: declare it
class CartViewModel @Inject constructor(private val analytics: Analytics) : ViewModel()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing a symptom (compile error) by moving code to common.
  • Copying NiA structure without NiA's team size or reasons.
  • Letting the module count grow with no pruning.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which one is most expensive to undo? → God common with api fan-out, because everything depends on it.
  2. How would you detect them automatically? → Graph checks, dependency analysis, module size budgets, build scans.
  3. Is a horizontal layer module ever fine? → For shared infrastructure (:core:network, :core:database), not for feature code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links each anti-pattern to a measurable signal and a cheap detection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A post-mortem showed 60% of cross-module PR friction came from three modules: common, data and ui, all horizontal layers.
